chief_complaint: sudden barking cough, squeaking breath noise, and low-grade fever at night
hpi_details: 3-year-old boy brought to ED at midnight due to sudden onset of a loud, barking cough that sounds like a seal. Had a runny nose for 2 days. Mother noticed a high-pitched sound when he breathes in (stridor).
ideas: mother terrified child is choking or suffocating
expectations: wants immediate relief for his breathing

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), parainfluenza is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), parainfluenza.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Epiglottitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Stridor at rest would indicate moderate-to-severe croup requiring epinephrine.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup), parainfluenza etiology
Administer dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously (maximum 10 mg); use local pediatric protocol
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

red_flags: Stridor at rest would indicate moderate-to-severe croup requiring epinephrine
Drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance, cyanosis, lethargy, or markedly increased work of breathing requires immediate emergency airway assessment

must_ask.say: Does his cough sound like a seal barking?

history.answer: He suddenly woke up coughing around midnight, and his cough sounds like a barking seal.
The loud barking cough started very suddenly tonight about two hours ago.
He had a mild runny nose and slight congestion for the past two days, but nothing like this.
It is a loud, harsh, barking sound that sounds like a seal or a dog.
The squeaking sound happens when he takes a breath in, especially when he cries or gets upset.
No, he has never had an episode of barking cough or breathing difficulty before.
His cough is dry and tight, with no sputum or phlegm coming up.
It started in the middle of the night, and his breathing always sounds worse when he is lying down asleep.
He does not have fits of non-stop coughing, and he has not vomited or made a whooping sound after coughing.
His breathing gets noisier and harder when he cries, but walking out into the cool night air seemed to ease it a little bit.
He seems to work harder to breathe, but I do not hear any chest wheezing like an asthma attack.
He felt a bit warm earlier tonight, and his temperature was 38.0 degrees Celsius when I checked it.
No, he has not coughed up any blood at all.
No, he was asleep in his crib when this started, and he was not playing with small toys or eating anything small.
No, he is not drooling, and he was able to swallow a little water without pain or trouble.
Yes, he has had a clear runny nose and a slightly stuffy nose for the past two days.
He has not complained of chest pain, though he looks startled and clutches his neck when coughing.
No, he has not had any weight loss or drenching night sweats.
No, he does not have sour regurgitation, heartburn, or persistent throat clearing.
No, his legs and ankles are completely normal with no swelling.
A couple of children in his daycare classroom had runny noses and mild coughs this past week.
He has no past medical problems and has always been a healthy child.
He has never had surgery and has never been admitted to a hospital.
He does not take any regular medications; I only gave him one dose of children's acetaminophen tonight for his fever.
He does not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or seasonal triggers.
There is no family history of asthma, reactive airway disease, or chronic lung conditions.
He was born at full term without any birth complications or oxygen support.
His growth and developmental milestones have all been completely on track.
He has received all recommended childhood vaccines on schedule, including his Hib and pneumococcal shots.
He attends a preschool program three days a week and lives at home with both parents, where no one smokes.
I was terrified he was suffocating, and I am anxious to know what breathing medication he needs to get relief right away.

exam.finding: Alert 3-year-old boy sitting comfortably on his mother's lap, producing a harsh seal-like barking cough and audible inspiratory stridor when agitated, with no cyanosis or drooling.
Temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Mild erythema of the posterior pharynx and clear rhinorrhea; no tonsillar exudate, uvula midline, and no excessive pooling of saliva.
Shotty, non-tender anterior cervical lymph nodes bilaterally; trachea midline with no masses.
Mild suprasternal and subcostal retractions noted during inspiration; symmetrical chest excursion without localized tenderness.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields bilaterally.
Audible inspiratory stridor transmitted from the upper airway; bilateral lung fields are clear with good air entry and no wheezes or crackles.
No clubbing or cyanosis of fingernails, and no lower extremity edema; warm peripheries with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
